system.sexual_systems: Monoecious individuals with unisexual flowers versus dioecious populations
system.geography: Southern Ontario, Canada, for original crosses/transplants; 2011 array-specific details not equated with 2004 cohort
system.unit_warning: Original cross families / ramets nested by 23 male or 27 female genotypes / environments / independent later mating arrays, NOT one linked fitness dataset

genetic_access_2004.citation: Dorken ME & Barrett SCH 2004, Proceedings of the Royal Society B 271:213–219
genetic_access_2004.access: Original PDF indexed searchable text, primary source PMC abstract; screenshot retrieval 403, printed table visual verification incomplete

selfed_inconstant_male.discrepancy: Unexpected all-hermaphrodite outcome, not explained by simple model

noted_departures.excess_f1_hermaphrodites: F1 241 pooled p=.01 vs 1:1 expected, not an across-study transition rate
noted_departures.multiple_f2_individual_crosses: Some isolated family G tests flagged in raw table, not significant after table-wide multiple-comparison adjustment

genetic_access_2004.inferred_sex_genetic_architecture: Mendelian linked two-locus sterility model consistent with many classes but not all; specific genes not molecularly sequenced in this original
genetic_access_2004.direct_access_scope: Experimental gamete/genotype combination to flowering phenotype and some F1 reproductive parent ability; not novel mutation or viable lifetime selection of every intermediate

sex_expression_resource_2004.remaining_low_genotypes_sex_state: NOT_EXACTLY_SPECIFIED_IN_EXTRACTED_TEXT; may contain mixed and/or not flower, so count expressing both low is between 0 and 2
sex_expression_resource_2004.interpretation: An observed same-genotype resource reaction norm on the male side; not a gain-of-function mutation rate or fitness benefit
sex_expression_resource_2004.source_text: Under high fertilizer 10/23 male genotypes produced male and female flowers; under low fertilizer 21/23 genotypes only male flowers; female genotypes did not produce male flowers

habitat_sorting_2003.evidence_level: Original abstract verified; no individual transplant survival counts extracted
design: common garden of sexual systems and F1 progeny
habitat_sorting_2003.monoecious_habitats: Disturbed ephemeral wetlands; shallow open settings
habitat_sorting_2003.f1_life_history_traits: Generally intermediate phenotype values, not a complete quantified mutational trajectory
habitat_sorting_2003.local_survival_results: Monoecious populations survive best in habitat matching unshaded origin; dioecious populations survive best in shaded origin; numeric survival ratios not extracted
habitat_sorting_2003.inference: Contemporary genotype-by-environment survival context for sexual-system backgrounds, not rare-mutant invasion experiment or demonstration of sexual-system origin

male_reproductive_performance_2011.evidence_level: Publisher/public abstract and accessible discussion excerpts; no raw genotype/seeds downloaded
male_reproductive_performance_2011.direct_design: Experimental mating arrays with female, male and hermaphroditic plants; paternity/siring success compared
male_reproductive_performance_2011.pollen_metering: Dioecious males displayed a smaller fraction of produced flowers simultaneously, prolonging pollen presentation compared with monoecious hermaphrodites
male_reproductive_performance_2011.reported_outcome: Siring success of males increased approximately linearly with male flower production in tested arrays, consistent with nonsaturating seasonal male payoff
male_reproductive_performance_2011.authors_caveat: Study does not directly estimate the shape of lifetime male fitness gain curve in long-lived clonal perennial
male_reproductive_performance_2011.inference: Population array performance, not natural lifetime relative success of all genotypes under multiple environmental partner frequencies

clonal_tradeoff_2012.citation: Van Drunen WE & Dorken ME (2012) New Phytologist 196:606–616
clonal_tradeoff_2012.evidence_level: Original public abstract, no raw common garden traits
clonal_tradeoff_2012.intervention: Common garden reproductive allocation manipulations in monoecious and dioecious origin plants
clonal_tradeoff_2012.observed_female_investment: Approx 1:1 biomass tradeoff between maternal sexual investment and clonal propagule production
clonal_tradeoff_2012.observed_male_investment: No equivalent detected biomass tradeoff for male function; higher nitrogen costs affect propagule nutrient content
clonal_tradeoff_2012.inference: Different resource currencies for female and male functions, not one universal scalar architecture K

cross_source_claim_limits: All 2004 F1/F2 source fractions are published rounded decimals, not integer counts; reconstruct feasible integer intervals only, do not fabricate exact raw phenotypes
Class_a F2 676 offspring from 8 crosses share parentage; do not count as 676 independent origins of sex differentiation
The two-locus explanation is a model inferred from segregation, not sequenced contemporary causal sex genes or measured spontaneous mutation paths
F2 and backcross progeny reaching flowering establish biological generation/accessibility, not lifetime viable fitness advantage of all intermediate genotypes

High and low fertilizer use clonally replicated genotypes but individual 23-genotype paired outcome identities are unavailable; derive only combinatorial directional bounds, not exact McNemar statistic or population-adjusted p
Female lack of sex inconstancy observed under these treatments is not permanent loss of all latent genomic competence in all environments
2003 transplant performance, 2004 crossing genetics, 2011 siring arrays and 2012 cost allocation are independent experimental cohorts; do NOT stitch into a same-individual causal fitness mediation
2004 F1 male×monoecious cross shows significant segregation skew, contrary to a perfect Mendelian narrative; F2 pooled tests match predicted genotype ratios
Sagittaria can have monoecy with UNISEXUAL flowers; these are NOT bisexual flowers, unlike protandrous Cyananthus or protogynous Pulsatilla
Sagittaria genetic cross demonstrates possible recombination between existing alleles; does not show new allele origin, establishment from rarity, or fixation through SLK ecological partner feedback
Different carbon/biomass versus nitrogen resource tradeoffs from 2012 are not empirically measured SLK module-building K or single unit
The original 2004 article PDF table was extracted as searchable text and abstract independently verified; web screenshot endpoint failed, so no new hidden exact phenotype counts asserted
